Description
The Biology Department at East Tennessee State University (ETSU) is seeking a motivated masters student starting fall 2027 to join Dr. Ryan Stephens' lab (https://ryanbstephens.wordpress.com). The Stephens’ lab focuses on understanding ecological interactions and community dynamics with a strong focus on trophic ecology of mammals and their consumption and dispersal of fungal spores and seeds. Graduate students will have the opportunity to work on projects involving both field research and lab-based studies, contributing to our understanding of ecological interactions and the functional roles that small mammals play in forested ecosystems. There is room for project development depending on the student’s interest with main research foci including 1) truffle-mammal interactions and the dispersal of fungal spores, 2) seed selection and dispersal by small mammals, and 3) trophic niche dynamics of small mammals.
 Position Requirements:
A bachelor’s degree in biology, ecology, environmental science, or a related field.
Previous research experience in ecology, natural resources, biology, or a related discipline is preferred.
·       Experience with field data collection, especially small mammal live trapping or taking forest compositional measurements is preferred but not required.
A valid US drivers license (or the ability to get one).
 Opportunities and Support:
The position is based at ETSU in Johnson City Tennessee and is available beginning August 2027. The ideal candidate will be able to start field data collection in May of 2027. Field work will take place in the Blue Ridge Mountains of East Tennessee. The Masters student will have support for 2 years including a tuition waver and stipend ($12,200) along with summer salary guaranteed in 2027.
 To apply, please email ([email removed]) your CV, statement of research interests (2 pages max), and contact information for three references. Include “Graduate student application” along with your last name in the email title. Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until the position is filled. To receive full consideration please apply before November 20, 2026. Please refer to https://www.etsu.edu/cas/biology/academics/ms_bio.php for information about the Biology M.S. program.

Position Description: I am seeking a master's student in Environmental Social Science to pursue a Master’s at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) to start in the Spring of 2027. Research will be supervised by Dr. Anna Erwin, assistant professor and environmental social scientist at UTRGV and director of the Environment and Society Research Group at UTRGV. Dr. Erwin has conducted social science research in diverse settings including the Andes and coastal regions of Peru with smallholder farmers, Indiana with migrant farmworker populations, the Southeastern US with a farmworker ministry, and the Lower Rio Grande Valley of TX with multiple agricultural actors.

In this project, you will be working with Dr. Erwin on a research project that involves a multi-state partnership, between Virginia and Texas, with the UTRGV team's work focusing on the LRGV of TX. You will conduct qualitative and quantitative case study research on relationships between farmers and farmworkers on small, sustainable farms in the LRGV of Texas. In particular, the prospective student will use social science methods (interviews, observations, and surveys) to investigate the relationships between farmers and farmworkers working on small farms. The goal of this research is to cultivate strategies to enhance the well-being of farmers and farmworkers working on small farms. This is a collaborative research project funded by the USDA that involves numerous local agricultural stakeholders, biophysical and social scientists, as well as faculty and staff from Virginia Tech. 

About the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley: UTRGV is a regional minority serving institution located in the southern tip of Texas along the US-Mexico border whose mission is to, "transform the Rio Grande Valley, the Americas, and the world through an innovative and accessible educational environment that promotes student success, research, creative works, health and well-being, community engagement, sustainable development, and commercialization of university discoveries.” It is also a binational and bicultural region that is also a hotspot for biodiversity of birds and insects, and in recent years has become a statewide mecca for sustainable and organic agriculture.

About the Masters of Science in Agricultural, Environmental, and Sustainability Sciences: The AESS program provides students with a unique, integrative education and training that prepares them to meet the challenges and opportunities in the multiple dimensions of sustainability sciences. This multidisciplinary degree program is designed to supplement theoretical understanding with action-oriented, applied research.

Requirements and compensation: The potential candidate will be expected to gather and analyze social science data from people during fieldwork in hot and humid subtropical climates. The student must also have a strong command of Spanish and English and a Bachelor's degree in biophysical or social science. Admissions are rolling. An annual salary of $27,450 will be available to the candidate and tuition support may be available. Additional support for research supplies, professional development, and travel to a relevant conference, as well as opportunities to participate in research projects outside of your own project, will be available. 

Contact and Application: If you are interested in this opportunity, please send a short introduction, a brief statement detailing your interest in this opportunity, and a CV/resume with coursework, GPA, and a list of names for 3 references to [email removed]

One Ph.D. Graduate Research Assistantship is anticipated at South Dakota State University beginning on or before January 2027 (flexible), contingent on candidate availability. This position will support a collaborative research project with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) Habitat and Population Evaluation Team (HAPET) to quantify the ecological value of small wetlands embedded in agricultural landscapes of the Prairie Pothole Region (PPR). Small wetlands comprise the majority of basins in the PPR and are central to conservation investments through programs, yet key uncertainties remain regarding their hydrology, disturbance, and functional importance to waterfowl and other wetland-dependent species. The successful candidate will serve as the primary coordinating scientist for an integrated research program that combines long-term datasets (e.g., Four Square Mile Waterfowl Breeding Survey), high-resolution remote sensing, and targeted field validation to address management-relevant questions at landscape to regional scales.
 The student will work closely with USFWS HAPET scientists and other partners to develop reproducible analytical workflows, conduct spatial and statistical modeling, and contribute to decision-support tools that inform wetland conservation prioritization. The position will include both computational and field components, including validation of remote sensing products and coordination of field data collection across the PPR.
 Qualifications: Applicants should have an M.S. degree in wildlife ecology, wetland ecology, natural resources, geospatial sciences, environmental science, or a closely related field. Exceptional candidates with a B.S. and strong quantitative skills may be considered.

3)      Quantitative skills (e.g., statistical modeling, programming in R or similar platforms).
4)      Ability to manage and integrate large, complex datasets.
5)      Experience or interest in applying machine learning or computer vision approaches.
6)      Capacity to coordinate fieldwork across large spatial extents.
 The position will involve interaction with federal and state agencies, NGOs, and private landowners; professionalism, strong communication skills, and the ability to work effectively and coordinate with diverse partners are essential.

Description
 Graduate Research Assistantship in Forest Biotechnology and Disease Diagnostics 

One M.S. or Ph.D. Position | Auburn University | Auburn, Alabama 

Why do some pine forests experience more severe disease than others? How do pathogen variation, host trees, and environmental conditions shape disease risk? Can we engineer better tools to detect disease before serious damage occurs? 

Auburn University is seeking one motivated M.S. or Ph.D. student to conduct interdisciplinary research at the intersection of forest biotechnology, molecular engineering, forest pathology, and disease ecology. The project will focus on brown spot needle blight of pine, caused by Lecanosticta acicola, with a central emphasis on engineering practical biotechnology tools for early disease detection and forest-health monitoring. 

The student will have opportunities to design, develop, and validate molecular diagnostic technologies for detecting the pathogen and assessing disease risk. Potential research areas include CRISPR-Cas12a–based diagnostics, aptamer-based biosensors, qPCR/ddPCR, functional genomics, molecular marker development, and bioinformatics. A major goal is to translate biological discoveries into field-compatible diagnostic tools that can ultimately support forest-health professionals and land managers. 

The student may also investigate how pathogen diversity, host characteristics, and environmental conditions influence disease development and severity, connecting biotechnology development with broader questions in disease ecology and forest health. 

Qualifications 

Applicants should have a bachelor’s degree in biotechnology, molecular biology, genetics/genomics, microbiology, bioengineering, biological engineering, plant pathology, forestry, forest biology, bioinformatics, or a related field. 

Strong academic preparation, curiosity, and the ability to work independently and collaboratively are important. Previous experience in molecular biology, PCR/qPCR, genomics, bioinformatics, biosensors, plant pathology, or related research is desirable but not required. 

Preference will be given to applicants with prior CRISPR/Cas, genome-editing, or CRISPR-based molecular diagnostic experience. Applicants with a master’s degree and/or GRE scores are also encouraged to apply.

Description
Graduate Research Opportunities
 in Pine Genetics and Forest Resilience

Two MS students or one PhD student at Auburn University

College of Forestry, Wildlife and Environment | Auburn, Alabama


How can genetics and planting decisions improve the pine forests we grow?
 Can beneficial fungi help pine seedlings survive and grow in salty soils?

Join our research team at Auburn University to investigate these questions and develop practical guidance for forest managers and landowners. We plan to recruit either two M.S. students, one for each project, or one Ph.D. student whose dissertation connects both research areas.

Faculty mentors: Dr. Hao Chen, Dr. Chris Anderson, and Dr. Ajay Sharma.


Project 1 Pine genetics and forest management

Use public genomic and trait datasets to investigate differences in loblolly pine growth, stem form, and wood properties. Develop genomic prediction and selection approaches, then combine forest growth modeling with economic analyses to compare genetic improvement scenarios, planting densities, and timber product outcomes. The goal is practical guidance for landowners and forest managers. This project emphasizes computational research using existing datasets.


Project 2 Pine establishment on lands affected by salinity

Test whether loblolly and slash pine genetic material and beneficial ectomycorrhizal fungi, which form partnerships with tree roots, improve establishment in salty soils. Through greenhouse experiments and field trials in Alabama, you will measure survival, growth, root development, fungal colonization, plant ion balance, and soil conditions. Findings will help identify promising pine–fungus combinations and guide planting practices on lands affected by salinity.


PhD option

The Ph.D. option connects genetic evaluation, seedling stress responses, fungal partnerships, and forest management. You will develop a focused dissertation with the advising team.


Qualifications and training

Applicants should hold a bachelor’s degree in forestry, biology, ecology, plant or soil science, natural resources, statistics, or a related field. Experience with R or Python, quantitative genetics, forest modeling, plant physiology, soil science, microbiology, or greenhouse and field research is welcome. We value curiosity, strong communication skills, and the ability to work independently and collaboratively. Prior research experience is particularly valuable for Ph.D. applicants.

Students will develop research and analytical skills, write a thesis or dissertation, and contribute to scientific publications and practical guidance for forestry stakeholders.


How to apply

Email a single PDF containing your CV, a one-page statement of research interests and career goals, unofficial transcripts, and contact information for three references. Description
The Ehlert and Brennan Labs are focused on developing high-quality, well-rounded leaders in rangeland ecology who produce strong research and possess the highly sought-after skill of effectively communicating science to land managers and stakeholders. We value rigorous field-based science, stakeholder-driven questions, and clear, applied outcomes.
 Project overview:
This Ph.D. project will examine the role of beaver dam analogs (BDAs) in prairie streams within the Northern Great Plains. Specifically, the goals of this project are to (1) use BDAs to improve riparian vegetation and function within a Northern Great Plains prairie stream; (2) incorporate VF technology to manage livestock grazing within pastures with active riparian restoration; and 3) develop a framework that integrates state and transition models with stream evolution models to promote greater adoption of riparian restoration at the landscape scale. This project fills an essential gap in knowledge on integrating innovative grazing solutions with riparian restoration efforts, ultimately improving natural resource management on stream miles across public and private landscapes. The student will contribute to study design, data collection and analysis, and outreach products, including peer-reviewed manuscripts, that translate findings into management-relevant insights.
 Responsibilities include:
·         Data collection on the effects of BDAs
·         Data collection and management of virtual fencing software 
·         Data management and analysis using R statistical software
·         Scientific writing, including a dissertation and peer-reviewed manuscripts
·         Stakeholder engagement and communication through workshops and Extension articles, etc. 
·         Professional development through conference presentations and networking
·         Adherence to SDSU research compliance requirements (IACUC)
 Required qualifications:
·         M.S. in rangeland ecology, natural resources, animal science, ecology, or a closely related field
·         Interest in riparian restoration, grazing management, virtual fencing, and applied research 
·         Strong work ethic, curiosity, and comfort working independently in rural field settings
·         Effective communication 
·         Strong time-management and ability to meet deadlines
·         Willingness to engage in stakeholder-driven research and applied outreach
 Preferred qualifications:
·         Previous experience working around/with beef cattle

·         Comfort troubleshooting challenges without constant direction

Description
Dr. Catrin Edgeley has funding available to support one M.S. student in the Department of Environment and Society at Utah State University. The student will contribute to a Joint Fire Science Program-funded research project focused on strengthening the scientific foundations of wildland fire investigations within federal and state land management agencies. This project is a collaboration between Utah State University, the Forest Stewards Guild, and USDA Forest Service researchers at the Missoula Fire Sciences Laboratory. Our interdisciplinary team will integrate social science, fire science, and practitioner expertise to improve understandings of the tools and indicators used to determine wildfire origin and cause. The student will play a key role in documenting the current state of wildland fire investigation science and practice by:

Conducting a review of federal fire investigation training materials, guidance documents, and related resources.
Designing and administering a national survey of wildfire investigators across agencies and organizations to understand current training needs and opportunities.
Spending several weeks at the Missoula Fire Lab during the summer of 2028 working with US Forest Service scientists on experimental research designed to evaluate fire pattern indicators and improve the scientific basis of wildland fire investigations.

The student will have opportunities to engage directly with practitioners and conduct to research with clear applications for wildfire prevention, management, and policy. They will contribute to peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, fact sheets, conference presentations, and other practitioner-oriented project deliverables.

The ideal candidate would be available to begin in Fall 2027, although there is some flexibility for a Spring 2027 or 2028 start date. This position is based at Utah State University's Logan campus and requires the student to attend in-person for the duration of their degree. The student will receive a nine-month academic year research assistantship for two years that includes an annual stipend between $24,000 and $27,000 depending on experience plus a summer stipend at a similar monthly rate in 2028, health insurance, and a full tuition waiver. The student will enroll in the M.S. Environment and Society program at Utah State University and develop a research-based thesis using data from tasks described above.

Required Qualifications
Bachelor's degree in natural resources, environmental studies, sociology, environmental policy, forestry, fire ecology, geography, criminal justice, or a related field before the start date.
Willingness to travel for fieldwork, trainings, professional meetings, or collaborator meetings, for up to several weeks at a time. 

Preferred Qualifications
Demonstrated interest in wildfire science, fire management, fire investigations, environmental policy, or applied social science.
Experience with qualitative and/or quantitative social science research methods.
Familiarity with software such as NVivo, Qualtrics, SPSS, ArcGIS Pro, or similar analytical tools.
Prior experience working for a federal or state agency in a role related to wildfire.
Strong written and oral communication skills.

Please note that eligibility is limited to U.S. citizens and permanent residents due to project funding and participation requirements.

To apply, please email the following materials to [email removed]:

A brief (<1 page) statement of interest for this position describing your background, qualifications, career goals, and interest in wildfire investigations or related topics.
A current CV or resume.
Unofficial transcripts.

Initial review of applications will begin November 16th 2026 and continue until the position is filled. Additional materials, including references and a writing sample, may be requested from shortlisted candidates.

Utah State University is the state's land-grant institution, serving more than 28,000 students across a statewide system. Logan is within easy access of numerous national forests, parks, and public lands throughout the Intermountain West.

Description
The Scordato Lab at Cal Poly Pomona invites applications for a Master’s student to study avian ecology in a Southern California agroecosystem. The Scordato lab is part of the SPACES Institute, a NASA-funded initiative aimed at integrating remote sensing data into on-the-ground assessments of biodiversity and ecosystem services. The SPACES Institute includes faculty from Cal Poly Pomona, UC Santa Barbara, and the UC Agriculture and Natural Resources extension. We work closely with farmers and conservation non-profits throughout our study region with the overall aim of improving biodiversity in complex agricultural landscapes.
 We are recruiting a Master’s student to study how native plant restoration and landscape-level vegetation structure affect avian communities across spatial scales. There is broad scope for the student to develop independent lines of inquiry, but any project will involve point counts in the field and use of remote sensing products. The student will have access to >4 years of longitudinal data on bird community structure, data on arthropod communities, newly collected high-resolution lidar and hyperspectral data, as well as existing NASA remote sensing products. The Master’s student will be expected to work on all aspects of the research project, collaborate closely with other members of our interdisciplinary research team, and lead the preparation of at least one peer-reviewed manuscript. The student will have opportunities to identify their own professional development priorities to advance their chosen career path. This position is funded for two years with the possibility of a third year. The expected start date is Fall 2027.
 Required qualifications: 1) a Bachelor’s degree in biology, ecology, environmental science, wildlife biology, or similar field; 2) strong writing and quantitative skills; 3) a valid US driver’s license.
 Preferred qualifications (but do not hesitate to apply if you do not have these): 1) experience with avian point counts and/or strong identification skills for Southern California birds; 2) experience conducting field research, particularly in challenging conditions; 3) familiarity with R and/or Python; and/or 4) experience working with geospatial data.
 Competitive applicants will be flexible, positive, and communicative during challenging fieldwork; enjoy data analysis and writing; and be passionate about communicating science to broad audiences. Our work involves extensive public outreach, and there are many opportunities to develop blogs, reports, and other media for the farming community involved in this project.

Description
The Merkle Research Group is looking for a highly motivated, creative, and field-capable Ph.D. student to lead a project studying how cattle grazing management using virtual fencing can potentially reduce risk of brucellosis spillover from elk to cattle. 

The project is a collaboration between Wyoming Game and Fish Department, the Beyond Yellowstone Living Lab, Greater Yellowstone Coalition, and University of Wyoming. The primary objectives include mapping areas of brucellosis spillover risk, comparing comingling risks before and after the implementation of virtual fencing, and quantifying direct interactions with behavioral observations in the field. However, the student will have the opportunity to shape and address additional management-related research questions. Data, some of which has already been collected, include cattle locations recorded by the virtual fencing collars and GPS ear tags, GPS collar data from elk, and field observations. 

Candidates must have a B.S. and preferably a M.S. degree in Ecology, Wildlife, Computing, or a related field. Applicants with experience managing and analyzing large spatial datasets (including remote sensing and animal movement data) in program R, conducting field work related to habitat and behavior, working independently and with a team on research projects, collaborating with wildlife managers and ranchers, and publishing peer-reviewed research will be favored. Successful applicants will be expected co-produce high-quality research with a collaborative team, present their work at professional conferences, and publish results in a timely manner in peer-reviewed journals. 

The successful applicant will be admitted through the Program in Ecology and Evolution at University of Wyoming. The student will be based in Laramie (USA), although field work during March-May for at least 2 years near Cody, WY will be required. A graduate assistantship will be provided, which includes tuition and benefits, and an annual stipend of $29,016. To apply, please email a SINGLE PDF file that includes 1) a detailed cover letter outlining, at a minimum, experience and interest in studying disease ecology and grazing management, field experience, and quantitative skills, 2) a CV, 3) contact information for three references, and 4) unofficial transcripts to Dr. Jerod Merkle ([email removed]) and Dr. Julie Brockman ([email removed]). Description

Graduate assistantship focused on population ecology of moose – we are seeking a highly motivated person to pursue a PhD degree in the Environmental and Life Sciences Graduate Program at Trent University in Peterborough, Ontario, Canada. The graduate student will join a large team implementing a field research project on the factors limiting and regulating moose populations in Ontario. The field project is a multi-year program that entails the GPS radio collaring of moose, American black bears, wolves and white-tailed deer to assess cause-specific mortality of moose and examine predator-prey dynamics. This project is entering its third year and has collected a large amount of data on moose vital rates and movements. We are seeking a student to focus their research on moose population dynamics and the drivers of variation in moose vital rates. Specific research questions will be determined collaboratively between the student and research team. The successful applicant will have considerable responsibility and freedom to formulate and address basic and applied research questions grounded in ecological theory. Field work will be highly varied and will include live trapping and deployment of collars on black bears, wolves and white-tailed deer and helicopter capture of adult and calf moose. Further, the project involves deployment of remotely triggered trail cameras, collection of non-invasive samples for black bear population estimation, vegetation surveys, hunter surveys, aerial population surveys and more. The student will be expected to conduct significant field work for their specific project AND assist in all field aspects of the broader project. The student will be co-supervised by Dr. Joe Northrup and Dr. Brent Patterson both of the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources & Trent University. 

 

Requirements

M.Sc. degree in ecology, wildlife biology, or related field is desired, but exceptional past experience may be considered in place of a M.Sc. degree. Applicants must meet the minimum entrance requirements for the Environmental & Life Sciences graduate program at Trent University.  Desired qualifications include a GPA >3.5 (4.0 scale). A strong background in ecology, demonstrated analytical capabilities, and passion for wildlife research are required. Strong quantitative, writing, and oral communication skills are also required. The strongest applicants will have demonstrated experience publishing in peer-reviewed journals, and with programming languages commonly used for statistical and scientific applications (e.g., R and Python), and familiarity with geospatial software (e.g., ArcMap, QGIS). Applicants should be physically fit, have significant field experience, be comfortable with flying in small planes and helicopters, and be capable of working in varied terrain for extensive periods in extreme conditions (e.g., temperatures that will range between 30 and -40 C, lots of biting insects etc.).

Application instructions

Initially, all applications are to be sent as follows. Please email a cover letter with an explicit statement of analytical/quantitative AND field experience and abilities, current CV, unofficial transcripts, scientific writing sample and contact info for ≥3 references as a single attachment to [email removed]. The successful applicant is expected to begin in spring or fall, 2027. Application deadline is November 15, 2026 but review of applications will begin immediately and continue until a suitable candidate is found. Once a successful applicant has been determined a formal application to the University is required, with a deadline of February 1, 2027.

 

Compensation

Students will receive a funding package of approximately $34,000 per year. This includes a combination of a graduate teaching assistantship, internal fellowships and a research assistantship. Further, during the first 2-3 years of the project, students working fulltime in the field will be provided shared housing. Tuition fees can be found here: https://www.trentu.ca/graduatestudies/financial-matters/student-account-and-tuition/research-and-thesis-based-program-fees. Numerous scholarships are also available and students are encouraged to apply (https://www.trentu.ca/graduatestudies/tuition-awards-funding/graduate-scholarships-and-awards). This funding package will not be reduced if a student is successful in obtaining a scholarship. 

Patterson and Northrup Labs

More information about the research groups of Drs. Brent Patterson and Joe Northrup can be found here: http://www.canidungulatelab.wixsite.com/brentpatterson and here: https://www.joenorthrup.com/. More information on the project can be found here: https://www.ontariomooseproject.ca/

 

 

Contact
Joe Northrup

Applicants should be physically fit, have significant field experience, be comfortable with flying in small planes and helicopters, and be capable of working in varied terrain for extensive periods in extreme conditions (e.g., temperatures that will range between 30 and -40 C, lots of biting insects etc.).

Application instructions

Initially, all applications are to be sent as follows. Please email a cover letter with an explicit statement of analytical/quantitative AND field experience and abilities, current CV, unofficial transcripts, scientific writing sample and contact info for ≥3 references as a single attachment to [email removed]. The successful applicant is expected to begin in spring or fall, 2027. Application deadline is November 15, 2026 but review of applications will begin immediately and continue until a suitable candidate is found. Once a successful applicant has been determined a formal application to the University is required, with a deadline of February 1, 2027.

 

Compensation

Students will receive a funding package of approximately $34,000 per year. This includes a combination of a graduate teaching assistantship, internal fellowships and a research assistantship. Further, during the first 2-3 years of the project, students working fulltime in the field will be provided shared housing. Tuition fees can be found here: https://www.trentu.ca/graduatestudies/financial-matters/student-account-and-tuition/research-and-thesis-based-program-fees. Numerous scholarships are also available and students are encouraged to apply (https://www.trentu.ca/graduatestudies/tuition-awards-funding/graduate-scholarships-and-awards). This funding package will not be reduced if a student is successful in obtaining a scholarship. 

Patterson and Northrup Labs

More information about the research groups of Drs. Brent Patterson and Joe Northrup can be found here: http://www.canidungulatelab.wixsite.com/brentpatterson and here: https://www.joenorthrup.com/. More information on the project can be found here: https://www.ontariomooseproject.ca/

Description
We are excited to offer a unique research assistantship opportunity focused on advancing the understanding of white rhino behaviour and ecology in South Africa.
WildComm is dedicated to conserving biodiversity on private land by creating opportunities for research, education, and hands-on conservation action. Our mission is
to demonstrate that private land can deliver both ecological and economic value, supporting wildlife and ecosystems beyond traditional protected areas. By joining
WildComm, you’ll be part of a growing network of researchers, students, and conservationists working together to generate vital ecological data, inform evidence-
based management, and inspire new models for wildlife conservation.

The project addresses urgent questions about the long-term impacts of dehorning on rhino behaviour. Most existing research is short-term or limited in scale, leaving important gaps in our understanding of how dehorning affects rhino. Using behavioural observations, we collect long-term data from reserves with different
management strategies. By comparing behaviour, habitat use, and social structure, we aim to support evidence-based conservation decisions for this iconic and endangered species.

Roles & Responsibilities
You will gain hands-on experience in wildlife research, contributing directly to this ongoing
study:
Tracking and locating individual rhinos on foot using spoor and field signs
Conducting extended behavioural observation sessions from safe vantage points
Recording systematic scan samples and filming focal individuals
Coding and analysing behavioural footage using standardised ethograms

Monthly Rate: £700 per person, including accommodation, research supervision and all necessary research equipment. Participants arrange their own travel, insurance and meals.

Willingness to work on foot over uneven terrain and in variable weather conditions
Moderate fitness level (endurance improves with experience)
Strong attention to detail and commitment to data management tasks
No prior field or rhino experience required

This research assistantship is ideal for students pursuing ecology, conservation biology, or related disciplines who seek practical, data-intensive field research experience in

USGS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), located at Bozeman, Montana.

The USGS mission is to monitor, analyze, and predict current and evolving dynamics of complex human and natural Earth-system interactions and to deliver actionable intelligence at scales and timeframes relevant to decision makers. As the Nation's largest water, earth, and biological science and civilian mapping agency, USGS collects, monitors, analyzes, and provides science about natural resource conditions, issues, and problems. 

Scientists at the Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center (NOROCK) in Bozeman, Montana conduct research on five general science research themes: 1) Biosurveillance of Biological Threats, 2) Wildlife Disease, 3) Fisheries and Water Resources, 4) Wildlife and Terrestrial Habitat, and 5) Cryosphere Science. 

Research Project: This is an opportunity to train with the Ecological Statistics (EcoStat) team based out of the Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center in Bozeman, MT. EcoStat team led and mentored by experienced collaborative research statistician, Dr. Kathryn M. Irvine. Broadly the EcoStat team engages in applied statistical research motivated by ecological problems relevant to conservation and management of the nation’s natural resources. Research projects are related to modeling spatial and temporally misaligned datasets in order to understand impacts of White-nose syndrome on bat species in the Western United States, research developing and testing statistical models for bat acoustic data, statistical evaluations of long-term, on-going monitoring of ecological indicators in Greater Everglades and beyond, statistical analyses for complex ecological data, and flexible, probability design creation for natural resource agencies.

Project activities include, but are not restricted to, developing and completing rigorous simulation studies to interrogate assumptions underlying statistical inferences stemming from choice of ecological model and monitoring design components, developing and testing novel statistical techniques that overcome inherent gaps in available methodology for analyzing real-world ecological data, creating transferable and reusable code with accessible documentation for practitioners, and/or visualizations of empirical and modeled results for communication with partners.

Project goals and objectives may include peer-reviewed manuscripts, collaborating on the creation and development of USGS software releases, and/or presenting novel research at professional meetings and conferences.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will gain experience within a premier natural science research agency and participating in large collaborative science teams. You will learn effective strategies for communicating with diverse science domain experts with varying levels of statistical training, techniques for conveying and explaining complex statistical information for non-statistical researchers, statistical collaboration skills with federal and state agency scientists, and how to pace projects and develop achievable milestones that demonstrate effective applied statistical practice. You are expected to be trained and become highly competent in statistical and data science skills (specific to your level of education) and the ability to communicate knowledge gaps early and acquire necessary technical skills independently and efficiently.

Description
Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission is recruiting candidates to fill the role of the Data Management Specialist 2 - Natural Coordinated Assessments and StreamNet. This is a full-time, full-year benefits eligible position located in Boise, Idaho. The anticipated start date is January 2027.
 
Position/Project Specifics:
The Coordinated Assessments Partnership (CAP) and StreamNet (SN) are collaborative efforts among federal, state, and tribal organizations creating access to standardized anadromous fish high level indicators (HLI) and fish monitoring metrics for informing regional assessments and reporting needs. The CAP has a hatchery origin component (HCA) and a natural component (NCA).

The data sharing achieved through the Pacific Northwest CAP and StreamNet projects inform decisions and reporting requirements that relate to both ESA-listed and non-listed salmon and steelhead, as well as other associated species.

This position will be primarily focused upon data extraction, transformation, and loading (ETL) into established data exchange structures (DES) for natural origin fishes. Additionally, they will aid in the development and testing of new data exchange structures both for natural and hatchery origin fishes.

The tasks related to achieving the objectives above will include communicating goals and needs of the project to biologists and research staff, collaborating with those personnel to locate appropriate data sources, and then developing workflows to ETL those data into the regional DES. The data will then be validated and uploaded to a shared, regional database. The workflows will be documented and shared with project personnel in order to build redundancy.

This position will also aid with meeting data and technical assistance requests for these data from internal and external customers. Some travel to regional offices may also be needed.

Essential Functions: (The functions listed below are characteristic of the type and level of work associated with this group and pay band. They are not all-inclusive. Individual positions may perform some or all, as well as other similar work.)
At the lower end of the range, employees:
· Compile natural resource project data into standardized electronic data formats. This includes accessing filed information and verifying its accuracy and completeness, performing data entry, electronic data transfer, editing, and error checking.
· Assist biologists with analyses and interpretation of data.
· Keep records on methods and parameters of data collection.
· Extract relevant data and present it in a variety of text and numeric formats, reports, tables, graphics, or figures.
· Maintain local versions of datasets in accordance with established regional database exchange formats and standards.
· Create queries, summaries, and/or maps for recurring reports.
· Ensure annual submittals for datasets are competed according to schedule
At the upper end of the range, employees:
· Standardize and automate workflows using SQL, ArcGIS Pro, R, and other software to streamline dataflow and provide quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC).
· Develop documentation and protocols using technical and non-technical formats.
· Work with internal and external collaborators, including state, federal, and tribal partners in a regional, consensus-driven environment.
· Attend technical and upper-level meetings for project direction and feedback. Take lead role on presenting information from biologist to technical committees for implementation into workflows.
· Supervising, mentoring and fostering the growth of a Data Management Specialist I working on Hatchery Coordinated Assessments Project.

Knowledge Required by the Position:
The employee must have knowledge and experience in:
· natural sciences
· personal computers and software packages and applications for databases, spreadsheets, and word processing
· data management concepts, principles, and methods
· quality assurance principles
· common query languages
· Supervising or mentoring
· MS SQL

sufficient to: input data; structure information retrievals; edit, combine and manipulate data; and/or provide reports for users. This knowledge allows the employee to assess or interpret the significance of the results and relate that to the overall objective of the assignment.

· R (including Shiny Apps and Markdown)
· Python (within a GIS environment)

 Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

Division of Marine Fisheries Management

OPS Fisheries & Wildlife Bio Scientist IV- 77909105

Duval

 

 

 

Our Organization:

The FWC envisions a Florida where fish and wildlife are abundant and thriving in healthy and connected natural landscapes with vital working lands and waterways; where natural resources are valued and safely enjoyed by all; and wherein natural systems support vibrant human communities and a strong economy.

Our Mission: Managing fish and wildlife resources for their long-term well-being and the benefit of people.

Every organization has an identity that is forged not only by what it does, but by how it conducts itself. The values embedded in our mission and expressed in the vision of the FWC are to make quality decisions by being dynamic, science-informed, efficient, ethical, collaborative, and committed to the vitality of the state and its environment. Visit our website for more information: MyFWC.com

 

Requirements:

Employment in this position is contingent upon a satisfactory criminal history check (fingerprint-based) in accordance with Chapter 435, Florida Statutes.

This is a Temporary position through June 30, 2027, with possibility of extension contingent on funding.

Must possess and maintain a valid driver’s license.

Monday – Friday, 8 a.m. – 5 p.m. Eastern Time.  Some travel is required and may include weeknights, weekends, and holidays.

 

Minimum Qualifications:

Six years of professional experience directly related to the duties and responsibilities provided herein. A post-secondary degree(s) in life or physical science may substitute for the required experience as follows: Bachelor of Science degree and two years of direct professional experience or a Master of Science degree and a minimum of one year of direct professional experience. Preference may be given to candidates with a Master of Science degree and one year of professional experience.

 

Overview:

The Commission expects its employees to be courteous and respectful while assisting Commission customers and stakeholders, ensuring each encounter is as positive as possible.  Employees should promptly resolve questions or problems relating to the Commission, its programs and/or fish and wildlife resources.  Employees should seek to gain public support for agency objectives and programs by serving Florida’s citizens in a positive and proactive manner and by listening to what the customer wants and striving to meet their needs.  When appropriate, employees will explain the reasons for agency actions or decisions while communicating a consistent FWC point-of-view.

 

Duties and Responsibilities:

Serve as a subject matter expert for state management of fisheries such as Gulf gag grouper.
Supports ongoing and future agency work on state management, including but not limited to fishery data collection, data analysis to inform state management efforts, development and refinement of outreach materials, conduct outreach and education, and assistance with responding to public inquiries.     
Develops and maintains productive working relationships with local fisheries stakeholders, including recreational and commercial fishermen, other state and federal agencies, and other groups or organizations with an interest in marine fisheries resources. 
Identifies and characterizes local marine fisheries management issues. 
Reviews and interprets fisheries dependent and independent data and other available scientific information to characterize the status of regional marine fisheries.
Assists with public workshops, Advisory Board/Workgroup meetings, and other information gathering meetings on issues relating to Florida's marine fisheries.
Assists division with fishery disaster assessments, including database development of active for-hire and commercial fishing operations in Florida, support with data analyses and writing fishery disaster reports.
Assists with the gathering and synthesizing of historical regulatory information to inform ongoing and future rulemaking and management decisions. Research historical management actions and decisions in support of division and agency staff.
Provides support to Section leaders, Deputy Director, and Division Director on special assignments as assigned.
Performs other related work as required.
 

 

Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities:

Knowledge of general biological principles and knowledge of marine fisheries management issues and topics;
Effective verbal and writing skills, ability to use good judgment in decision-making and planning skills;
Ability to synthesize highly technical information for public dissemination;
Ability to understand, evaluate, analyze and organize marine resource (especially fisheries) information into a logical format for presentation in reports, documents and other written materials and for coherent presentations to a variety of audiences;
Ability to plan, organize, coordinate and complete work assignments;
Ability to conduct fact finding research and utilize problem solving techniques;
Ability to review and interpret fisheries regulations;
Ability to establish and maintain effective working relationships with diverse groups of people;
Ability to work independently and as part of a team. Position synthesizes technical fisheries assessment information in support of the agency’s marine fisheries management process, evaluates life history and fisheries-dependent and independent data, and develops reports and presentations on marine fisheries issues.
Must be willing and able to travel and work overtime hours, including some weekends, weeknights, and holidays. 
Knowledge of computer software including Excel spreadsheets, MS PowerPoint and MS Word required.

Description
Two volunteer/intern field assistant positions are available 20 Feb to 15 Jun 2027, to take part in an ongoing behavioral study of female mate choice and male display behavior in Lance- tailed Manakins (Chiroxiphia lanceolata) in Panama. These positions are designed to maximize training opportunities for post-graduate students who are seeking experience in basic science research as they consider applying to graduate school.

Research background: Females of this small, lekking bird “shop” among males that display in cooperative pairs on dispersed display areas. Successful applicants will be involved in work investigating how strong sexual selection is changing this wild population over time, how male experience affects display performance and cooperative behavior, why dominant males tolerate subordinate cooperators, and how indirect genetic benefits affect female mate choice and maternal investment.

Responsibilities and qualifications: All field crew members will take part in resighting color- banded birds, conducting many hour-long behavioral observations at display sites, daily maintenance of a video detection system, nest-searching through dense secondary-growth dry tropical forest, and mistnetting birds for banding and blood sampling, as well as data entry and organizational tasks. Experience in one or more of these areas is strongly preferred. Applicants should have a very strong interest in animal behavior, birds, and field biology. The full field crew is a 4-5 person team of researchers who will live and work on a remote island off of Panama's Pacific coast and share housing with close quarters. The site provides internet access and cell phone reception, but unpredictable power outages can happen and last for days. In addition to the usual need for experience working in isolated field settings and/or shared living situations with little privacy, applicants should be level-headed, resilient, and responsible to work safely and thrive during their time with this project. Team members should be comfortable engaging respectfully with the local community, including through our annual outreach day at the local primary school.

This is a demanding six-day-per-week field position; in addition to scheduled data collection (approximately 30 hours/week), it also entails long hot hikes to reach data collection sites,  data entry and organization requirements, and shared household responsibilities that require daily effort, making this a full-time commitment while in the field. Applicants should be enthusiastic, physically fit, and emotionally grounded. Expect to work long days, be woken at 4 am by howler monkeys on a regular basis, and see some amazing bird behavior. A sense of humor, ability to work independently, and willingness to accommodate unpredictable changes is especially important. Conversational Spanish ability is strongly preferred for this position. Assistants are also required to complete online animal care and use training shortly after being hired.

Compensation: Food, housing, and required transportation within Panama will be provided, as well as a $1500 honorarium upon completion of the field season to help defray costs of health insurance and personal purchases. Assistants will also be reimbursed for round-trip airfare to Panama City, Panama (up to $750) upon completion of the field season, and will need to provide their own snake gaiters (~$50) and to follow any Covid testing/vaccination requirements for travel.
For more information about the research see ( http://www.bio.fsu.edu/duval/ ). Ongoing outreach efforts associated with this work include a live-streaming webcam of manakin activity run in collaboration with the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and archived footage from previous years can be viewed here:  https://www.allaboutbirds.org/cams/lance-tailed-manakins/ .

To apply complete please complete this google form:  https://forms.gle/7pVWVkUtRCk8bbYn8 
You will be asked to upload your CV, and provide contact information for 3 references, as well as answering a series of prompts comparable to a coverletter summarizing your experiences and interest in the job. Panamanian citizens are encouraged to apply, and assistants not requiring airfare to reach the Republic of Panama would receive a modestly increased personal honorarium. Review of applications will continue until positions are filled. If you encounter problems with the form, you may email application materials to Emily DuVal (EM: ehduval AT fsu.edu) with the subject line "Lance-tailed Manakin Field Crew Application".

Additional questions may be directed to DR. EMILY DUVAL, (EM: ehduval AT bio.fsu.edu) or KAYA SIMMONS (EM: kes22g AT fsu.edu), Florida State University Department of Biological Science. Please use the subject line “Lance-tailed Manakin field crew application.”

U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM)
Rangeland Management Specialists | GS-5 through GS-11
Permanent • Full-Time • Multiple Locations

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) will soon be advertising permanent Rangeland Management Specialist positions (GS-5 through GS-11) at multiple locations across the West.

If you're interested in rangeland management, livestock grazing, wildlife habitat, vegetation management, natural resources, and public lands, this is an opportunity to build a long-term career managing some of the nation's most iconic landscapes.

What will you do?

BLM Rangeland Management Specialists work at the intersection of science, land management, people, and policy. Depending on the position and location, work may include:
Managing livestock grazing on public lands
Conducting rangeland and vegetation monitoring
Evaluating rangeland health and ecological conditions
Working with ranchers, grazing permittees, and local communities
Managing wildlife habitat and other natural-resource values
Developing and implementing rangeland management plans and projects
Using GIS, data, and other technology to support land-management decisions
Working with interdisciplinary teams on complex natural-resource issues
Spending significant time in the field on public lands

The work is a combination of fieldwork, science, collaboration, analysis, and resource management. Some days may be spent in the field evaluating vegetation and grazing conditions; other days may involve analyzing data, working with partners, or developing management recommendations.

Who should consider applying?

We are interested in reaching students, recent graduates, and experienced natural-resource professionals who meet the federal qualification requirements for the 0454 Rangeland Management Specialist series.

Your degree does not necessarily have to be titled "Rangeland Management." Depending on your coursework and experience, degrees in related natural-resource fields may qualify.

Positions are expected to be advertised at GS-5 through GS-11, providing opportunities for individuals at different stages of their careers.

Why BLM?

A career with BLM provides the opportunity to work directly on America's public lands while building a career in natural-resource management.

BLM employees work across some of the most diverse landscapes in the country and collaborate with ranchers, communities, Tribes, other agencies, conservation organizations, and the public to manage these lands for multiple uses and sustained resource health.

This isn't just a summer job or internship—these are permanent positions with opportunities to build a career in public-land management.

Coming Soon — Start Preparing Now

The vacancy announcement is expected to be open for a limited period, potentially as little as 14 days. If you're interested, we encourage you to start preparing your application materials now rather than waiting for the announcement to open.

Once the announcement is posted, applicants will need to apply through USAJOBS and meet the specific qualification and application requirements listed in the vacancy announcement.

Questions or Need Help Preparing?

Please feel free to contact me before the announcement opens.

I am happy to answer questions about the positions, the BLM work environment, the application process, or how to prepare for a federal application.

If you're a student or recent graduate and aren't sure whether your education or experience may qualify for the 0454 series, please reach out. I would rather have you ask questions ahead of time than decide not to apply because you're unsure whether you qualify.

GENERAL DESCRIPTION:
Under the direction of the Conservation Program Director, this position performs highly complex (senior level) administrative and supervisory program work. Leads a team of seven statewide taxonomic experts and a conservation initiatives specialist to "conserve and recover imperiled species and habitats through research, management, policy, and partnerships." Represents the Department at state and national levels in matters pertaining to SWAP implementation. Reviews technical reports and management reports to support science-based decision making. Builds and maintains cooperative relationships with TPWD staff and external partners to build capacity for on-the-ground projects tied to implementation of the SWAP and to fulfill federal aid requirements. Builds and maintains cooperative relationships with TPWD staff and external partners - including agencies, NGOs, land trusts, joint ventures, and planning entities - to advance conservation and integrate SWAP priorities. Description
Life Net Nature Ecuador Bird Monitoring Expedition A Cost-share Volunteer Training Experience

Learn or improve bird banding and monitoring skills in the tropical Andes mountains of western Ecuador. Help advance science about tropical montane forest bird communities. Learn how to collect data to determine community and species-level responses to deforestation, forest recovery, forest fragmentation, and landscape and climate changes. Your participation helps sustain an important protected area in the mega-diverse Choco Endemic Bird Area (EBA). 

Cost-share volunteers/trainees assist Dr. Dusti Becker with long-term avian monitoring and conservation in the Andes at the beautiful forest protected area, Reserva las Tangaras.  In exchange volunteers receive experience-based training in mist netting and bird banding, including the use of Hall traps and practice with some aspects of hummingbird banding. 

Team Dates:     December 7-20, 2026 (1 position available).    Meets in Quito 8:45 am at Posada del Maple on 7th. 

Where:  Reserva Las Tangaras, a 130-acre nature preserve, boasts more than 25 species of hummingbirds, dozens of colorful tanagers, the largest regional Andean cock-of-the-rock display lek, along with over 300 tropical bird species, many of which are Choco and Andean endemics. During the expedition, LNN teams typically detect around 175 - 200 different species of birds in the reserve and study area. Team members will see additional bird species while traveling to and from the project site. The reserve is also home to endangered capuchin monkeys, spectacled bears, cougars, and myriads of other wildlife species, including several rare and endangered reptiles and amphibians. 

Activities: Volunteers are trained (or refreshed on) setting up and monitoring mist nets, extracting birds from nets, carrying birds from nets to a banding station, and recording ornithological and ecological data in the field. Volunteers are also trained to band birds and make standard measurements of birds. Volunteers also learn about Hall trapping and banding hummingbirds. The site is rugged, requiring above average fitness including: ability to hike on steep, potentially muddy and slippery terrain, and cover 2-4 miles on foot each day. Back or joint impairments, or obesity may make the project too challenging for some. 

Volunteers will have time to explore the Mindo area, and the team visits higher-elevation Bellavista Cloud Forest Reserve on the last day before returning to Quito. The December team will participate in the Mindo Christmas Bird Count (CBC), which typically wins first or second place globally for bird species counted. 

Food and Lodging: Accommodation is in a spacious research cabin, where each participant has a single bed mattress with mosquito netting, pillow, and fitted sheet. Two showers with hot water and flush toilets provide comfortable field accommodations. Meals are delicious, home-style Ecuadorian, prepared by excellent cooks, and vegetarian diets can be accommodated. 

COST: Your contribution of $2450 covers transportation during the field project to and from Quito,Ecuador, meals at RLT, lodging at RLT, reserve entrance fees, salaries for Ecuadorian cooks and para-biologists, leader's costs, and a special lunch at the Bellavista Reserve. Airfare to and from Quito, Ecuador and expenses in Quito before and after the expedition are not included. Meals away from RLT during project day off are not included. 

Your cost-share helps sustain Reserva las Tangaras, supporting year-round stewardship, educational programs, outreach materials about cloud forest wildlife, maintenance of trails and signs, cabin repairs, and feeding of resident hummingbirds. Cost-share donations are used to operate the 2-week field expedition: providing the team with food, shelter, training and transportation, as well as purchasing new project equipment and supplies. 

This exciting conservation expedition begins and ends in Quito, Ecuador. Volunteers should be in Quito at least 24 hours before meeting on the morning of December 7. Optional meet up for dinner on the 6th. 

Contact Dr. Dusti Becker, [email removed], for further details and to obtain a Life Net Nature volunteer application form.

Professionals and retirees in field biology, will enjoy the "field camp" experience and are much appreciated for their co-mentoring and experiences they share. All participants have the option of using the > 20 year project database for research publications, undergraduate projects, or graduate degrees.  

Visit https://lastangaras.wordpress.com/who-are-we/ for more details about Life Net Nature and Reserva Las Tangaras.

Description
 Postdoctoral Researcher in Mountain Lion Population Genetics 
Nevada Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit & University of Nevada, Reno 
 Project description and responsibilities: We seek a Postdoctoral Researcher to lead a project quantifying mountain lion population genetic structure and landscape connectivity across Nevada. The postdoc will be based out of the Nevada Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit (NVCFWRU) in the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences (NRES) at the University of Nevada, Reno (UNR). Project objectives include estimating statewide population genetic diversity and differentiation, effective population sizes, and identifying the landscape drivers of genetic connectivity. The ideal candidate will have experience generating and analyzing genome-wide datasets and be able to develop/implement code (e.g. python, R) for raw data processing, estimating standard population genetic metrics, and integrating genomic data with spatial datasets. The postdoc will be expected to work closely with state agency staff, produce project reports, publish at least one peer-reviewed journal article, give presentations to cooperators and at professional conferences, and supervise project data management. 
The Postdoc will work on campus and be co-advised by Drs. Brian Folt and Marjorie Matocq. The Postdoc will be an integral part of our lab communities and will have opportunities to engage in mentoring, grant writing, developing research collaborations, and other aspects of professional development. Our lab communities are committed to the development of early-career scholars and we value intersectional diversity and work-life balance. 
 Qualifications: PhD in population genetics, wildlife biology, conservation biology, or a related field. Applicants must have experience in generating and analyzing genome-wide datasets (e.g. ddRAD or WGS) and conducting standard population genetic analyses. Candidates must have strong oral and written communication skills and must have strong data management skills. Preferred candidates will have knowledge of mammalian ecology and management, as well as a strong record of publishing peer-reviewed literature.

Description
Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission is recruiting candidates to fill the role of a Fishery Biologist located at the USGS Columbia River Research Laboratory in Cook, WA. This position is considered full time, with a contract lasting one year that is likely to be extended from year to year. The preferred candidate should be able to accommodate a flexible schedule during the field season. This includes either 4 days on, 3 days off, 5 days on with weekends off, or an occasional 8 day on, 6 day off schedule as necessary, depending upon field activity. Winter schedule is typically a standard 5 day work week with weekends off, with some flexibility.
 
This project is designed to monitor fishery response of ESA listed Chinook salmon, steelhead, and bull trout relative to habitat conservation actions that are being implemented throughout the Columbia, Snake, and Sacramento river basins. Data generated from these studies will be used to further understand and evaluate the relationship between habitat capacity and freshwater survival and will help guide future restoration efforts using an adaptive management approach.
 
The selected candidate will be responsible for leading and conducting a range of field work activities aimed at evaluating life stage specific abundance and survival, including backpack and barge electrofishing, operating and maintaining rotary screw traps, operating adult fish traps and weirs, radio and acoustic telemetry, spawning ground surveys, PIT tagging of juvenile and adult salmonids, PIT tag array operation and maintenance, collecting biological samples, and collecting physical habitat data such as water temperature, flow, and general habitat characteristics. Office duties will include data organization and entry, data quality control, database management, assisting the lead USGS biologist in data summary, and preparation of figures and maps. The selected candidate will participate as a member of a research team conducting studies throughout western North America.

Applicants should be detail-oriented with a strong work ethic, organized, self-motivated, and able to work independently with little supervision. Previous experience with methods described above that are used to monitor freshwater life stages of anadromous fish is preferred. Applicants should be proficient with word processing, spreadsheet software, and databases.
 
Essential Functions:   
At the lower end of the range, Fishery Biologists have a solid working knowledge of established scientific methods and techniques to perform recurring assignments of moderate difficulty.  Methods and techniques are well established, apply to most situations, and do not require significant deviations.  Resource planning reports generated by employees at this level involve conventional biological concerns.  Reports generated may be short-range management plans or portions of annual work plans.  Lower range work examples include:
Following existing protocols for fish health screenings, conduct tissue sample collection, bacterial testing and analyses, blood collection and analyses, parasite identification, and necropsies on experimental fish populations.
Recommend modifications of existing research protocols.
Design data collection forms and set up research databases for integration of data.
Compile and analyze data for reports, prepare graphics, contribute to or write papers for peer-reviewed journals, and present research results at professional meetings.
Plan, schedule, and conduct behavioral, physiological, morphological, and survival evaluations of hatchery and/or experimental fish populations.
Oversee and assist with fish culture tasks for study purposes and recommend procedure variations. Write or contribute to papers and reports for publication, and compile reports on results of data collection and analysis.
Prepare and deliver formal and informal presentations at seminars, meetings, etc.
Work with state, federal and regional fishery management councils to provide data on fisheries catch and effort and population trends as well as biology of marine fish species.
Conduct limited physical and biological watershed, stream, and fish habitat assessments. Responsible for conducting data investigation and research, drafting technical report, database management, GIS for all physical and biological data, and survey and inventory results.
At the upper end of the range, the Fishery Biologist has specialized knowledge and demonstrated competence in advanced techniques of a complex area of fish biology sufficient to serve as a troubleshooter or specialist.  The employee is competent to modify or adapt standard techniques, processes and procedures, and to assess, select, apply precedents and devise strategies and plans to overcome significant problems related to species production, protection, habitat restoration, or program management and evaluation. Planning reports generated by employees at this level assess the impact of various multi-faceted management or public practices on a resource. Upper range work examples include:

Use biological information to evaluate run profiles and habitat suitability in stocked streams within a major geographical area.
Develop comprehensive management plans to insure preservation, protection, and enhancement of habitats.
Plan, design and implement research studies on fish health and/or nutrition.
Analyze and report biological and/or genetic information affecting future selection, rearing, and spawning activities.
Prepare both quarterly progress and annual reports on run status and hatchery or fish facility operations.
Monitor and evaluate hatching, rearing and planting of fish.
Evaluate and monitor adult return rates.
Develop new rearing strategies.
Prepare fish habitat measurement plans or management plans for a watershed or large geographic area.
Diagnose various fish diseases or nutritional disorders in experimental populations or brood stock. Develop modifications to existing health protocols as well as experimental protocols.
Write publishable reports of research and project findings.
Knowledge Required by the Position: 

Knowledge of fishery biology (including knowledge of particular species of fish) .
Knowledge of fish husbandry.
Knowledge of aquatic habitats.
Knowledge of the scientific method.
Knowledge of sampling protocols.
Knowledge of Windows-based computer applications such as word processing, spreadsheets, e-mail, publishing software, presentation software, database software, topographic software, bibliographic software, and statistical analysis packages.
Knowledge of technical writing protocols.
Knowledge of advanced statistical analysis and mathematics.
Additional Mandatory Skills:  

lift 40-50 lbs.                                            
valid driver's license
habitat typing                                     
habitat monitoring                  
fish ageing (scale, otolith, other)        
fish species ID skills               
specific software (spreadsheet, word processing, database management, GIS, statistical analysis, behavioral analysis, bibliographic)
oral communication skills                              
written communication skills              
Physical Demands:
Demands generally range from sedentary to moderate --where there is walking, climbing stairs and ladders, reaching, lifting, bending, or extended periods of standing. Some Fishery Biologists in this range have rigorous physical demands where they must be able to handle buckets of water or gear weighing from 40 - 50 pounds, engage in long daily periods of hiking, camp out for extended periods, or maintain footing in fast-moving water.

Work Environment:
Some work is performed in an office setting with adequate lighting, heating and ventilation. Some work may be performed in a laboratory setting which exposes the biologist to odors, chemicals, fish blood, and molds. The employee must use safety precautions including MSDS, gloves, hood, and eye protection. Some employees may work on narrow, elevated walkways and platforms that are over or adjacent to water. Field work involves exposure to all types of weather, slippery rocks or docks, trails, irregular terrain, insects, poison oak, rough or fast-moving water, or cold water temperatures. Work at high elevations or aboard boats may be required.


Qualifications
Minimum Qualification Requirements:
A range of education and experience may be presented.

At the lower end of the range, candidates must present successful completion of a full 4-year course of study in an accredited college or university leading to a bachelor's or higher degree that included a major in biological science with at least 6 semester hours in aquatic subjects and at least 12 semester hours in the animal sciences.  In addition to the undergraduate degree requirement, candidates for positions at the lower end of the range must also present 1 year of Specialized Experience** OR 2 years of progressively higher graduate education leading to a master's degree in fields directly related to the position being filled. An equivalent combination of experience and education is also qualifying.

At the upper end of the range, in addition to the undergraduate course of study described above, candidates must also must present one year of Specialized Experience**  OR  3 years of progressively higher level graduate education leading to a Ph. About SIG-NAL: 
SIG-NAL is a non-profit dedicated to advancing science, policy, and practice for resilient landscapes and communities. We pilot and scale innovations in environmental management that span urban and natural landscapes by connecting cutting-edge analytics with policy and planning to deliver solutions for a more resilient future. For over a decade, we’ve partnered with agencies on data-driven strategies for ecological restoration and nature-based solutions that benefit people and nature. Our work supports resilient cities, fire-adapted communities, sustainable land management, global conservation partnerships, environmental monitoring, and biodiversity conservation. 

Resilient Cities Program: 
We believe that healthy urban landscapes are essential for thriving, equitable cities. By building long-lasting partnerships with communities, we facilitate the reimagining of urban environments as vibrant, multifunctional spaces that support people, plants, and wildlife. Our Resilient Cities Program fosters strong network connections across disciplines, enabling us to translate science into innovative policy and practice, creating lasting solutions that sustain cities and restore the natural systems they depend on. 

Position Overview:  
The Program Manager will support the strategic initiatives of our Resilient Cities Program. The primary focus will be mainstreaming Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI) in Cities and Towns across the Southwest US, and a secondary focus supporting state and local water policy. Some in-person meetings and fieldwork required. There may also be infrequent travel and occasional weekend or evening hours. 

Desert Southwest communities face two linked challenges: intensifying urban heat and strained water supplies. GSI offers a direct answer to both. By directing stormwater runoff to trees and vegetation via passive rainwater harvesting, it turns a waste stream into a resource, cooling neighborhoods, replenishing soil moisture, and supporting conservation goals, while delivering co-benefits like better air quality, reduced flooding, and stronger community well-being.

Our approach: integrating GSI best practices into municipal projects and policy; tackling the maintenance challenge and building workforce capacity; and accelerating residential rainwater harvesting.

Community-based residential rainwater harvesting initiatives
State and local policy work advancing water quality and conservation

SUMMARY:
The Hatchery Maintenance Technician leads facility maintenance and grounds care at the LTBB Fisheries Enhancement Facility while executing advanced aquaculture and research operations. Operating under the direction of the Hatchery Manager, this position oversees the maintenance of Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS), live feed production, outdoor pond culture, and routine fish propagation. Additionally, the Hatchery Maintenance Technician collaborates within the Great Lakes Program to assist with research design, protocol development, data management, and operational upkeep to ensure peak facility performance. The exclusive purpose of this position is to work in Whitefish and Whitefish related restoration activities, supported by the Great Lakes Fisheries Trust Directed Lake Whitefish Funding Initiative.

ESSENTIAL DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES:

Facility & Mechanical Maintenance
Lead the facility maintenance and infrastructure upkeep program for the hatchery.
Oversee the continuous operation, troubleshooting, and preventative maintenance of Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS), pumps, filtration units, and bio-filters.
Perform routine inspections and preventative maintenance on department vehicles, machinery, and equipment on site.
Execute basic mechanical, electrical, HVAC, and plumbing repairs as needed across all facility systems.
Maintain strict biosecurity by cleaning, disinfecting, and maintaining hatchery holding tanks, trucks, nets, field gear, and working areas.
Participate in a scheduled on-call rotation to respond to facility alarms and emergencies during off-hours as assigned.

Hatchery Operations & Fish Culture
Assist with all phases of fish culture, including egg collection, incubation, fry and fingerling rearing, and fish stocking activities.
Cultivate and maintain live feed cultures (e.g., zooplankton, Artemia, bloodworms, algae) to support aquaculture research and species propagation.
Assist with the outdoor rearing pond culture program, including routine water quality monitoring (dissolved oxygen, temperature, pH) and fish health tracking (growth, weight, disease monitoring).
Conduct biological subsampling programs and provide logistical support for fish health testing.

Fieldwork & Sampling
Assist in fish gamete collection using a variety of gear types (e.g., gill nets, seines, impoundment nets, electroshocking).

Research, Data & Administration
Collaborate with the Hatchery Manager, Great Lakes Fisheries Manager, or Natural Resource Director to research operational topics and develop culture methodologies for new target species.
Process biological samples and maintain detailed, accurate logs of research and production data.
Assist the Hatchery Manager with preparing operational reports, data summaries, and presentations.
Utilize specialized software and technology to manage records, map data, and track operations (e.g., ArcGIS, QCapture, Microsoft Excel, Word, Access, R, QGIS).
